I've been farming these 16.9 mu for 50 years now. I'm 73 this year, and I can't work like I used to, but I still know every inch of this land. My son and daughter-in-law work in a factory in Shijiazhuang and send some money home, which helps with buying inputs, but I'm still careful with every yuan — old habits don't change. My wife and I do most of the farm work, and my grandson helps when he's back from school.

It's early October, so I'm getting ready to plant winter wheat. I'll sow around October 10th, after the maize harvest is fully cleared. I use an improved wheat variety — I bought fresh seed two years ago and I've been carefully selecting my own seed since then, but the yield has stayed good, about 420 kg per mu last year. Before planting, I'll spread about 50 kg of compound fertilizer per mu as base dressing, then harrow it in. Come late March, when the wheat starts jointing, I'll topdress about 20 kg of urea per mu. The extension agent says 15 kg nitrogen per mu is enough, but I've seen that 16-17 kg gives me more stable yields, and at my age I'm not taking risks — a little extra fertilizer is cheaper than a bad harvest. I'll irrigate three times: once before winter if the soil is dry, once at green-up in early March, and once at jointing. Pumping water costs more than it used to, so I won't waste it.

The summer maize is always a rush — after wheat harvest around June 8th to 10th, I have less than a week to get the maize in the ground before the season slips away. I hire a tractor for light rotary tillage and plant hybrid maize seed right away. I put down about 40 kg of compound fertilizer per mu with the seed, and topdress with about 15 kg of urea per mu when the corn is at the big trumpet stage. Two irrigations should be enough if the summer rains are normal — one at tasseling and one at grain filling. I always watch for corn borer; that pest cost me nearly 100 kg per mu two years ago, so I spray insecticide and put down herbicide at planting.

My family puts in about 24 days of labor across both crops, mostly for fertilizing, irrigating, and managing the harvest. I hire about 7 days of labor for the peak rush — wheat harvest, maize planting, and maize harvest — because I can't keep up at my age. I'm hoping for 420 kg per mu on wheat and 480 kg per mu on maize. If the weather holds and prices don't collapse, that should cover my costs and leave enough for the household.
